summary.p1: Muu Blanco (Caracas, Venezuela, 1966) is a multidisciplinary artist, video artist, and creator of multimedia installations based in Miami. Since the early 1990s, his practice has explored the relationship between image, sound, and the urban landscape through experimental video, sound art, performance, photography, and video mapping.
summary.p2: His early video works were produced using the Video8 format and later presented at the II Pirelli Salon of Young Artists at the Museum of Contemporary Art of Caracas, where the complete series was acquired by the Noa Noa Collection. His work has been exhibited in institutions such as the Museum of Contemporary Art of Caracas Sofía Imber, Sala Mendoza, the National Cinematheque of Caracas, and Mandragoras Art Space in New York.
summary.p3: Since relocating to Miami in 2014, Blanco has continued developing multimedia installations integrating video mapping, sound art, and performance, including his recent project NatuUrban Symphony (2024–2025).

full.p1: Muu Blanco (Caracas, Venezuela, 1966) is a multidisciplinary artist, video artist, and creator of multimedia installations based in Miami. His artistic practice encompasses experimental video art, sound art, performance, photography, assemblage, installation, electronic music, and video mapping, developing since the early 1990s an ongoing investigation into the relationship between image, sound, and the urban landscape.
full.p2: Blanco began working with experimental video art in the early 1990s, initially using the Video8 format as a tool for aesthetic exploration. His first participation in a collective exhibition with video took place in 1992, when one of his pieces was acquired by the collector Jimmy Belilty. From that moment, he began a continuous exploration of experimental audiovisual language.
full.p3: In 1994 he participated in the group exhibition Mixed Techniques at Alternative Gallery in Caracas, one of his earliest presentations within the contemporary art exhibition circuit.
full.p4: By 1995 he had produced more than thirty experimental video pieces, which were later presented at the II Pirelli Salon of Young Artists (1997) at the Museum of Contemporary Art of Caracas, where the entire group of works was acquired by the private Noa Noa Collection of the Oberto family.
full.p5: During the late 1990s and early 2000s he continued expanding his audiovisual research, documenting performances and developing experimental projects in video and sound.
full.p6: In 2002 he participated in the exhibition From White Cube to Black Box: Historical Tapes, Creative Videos, Digital Art, Venezuelan Video at the Museum of Contemporary Art of Caracas Sofía Imber. That same year he also participated in the project Multimedia Artist, Founder of the Center for the Arts, presented at the same institution. During this period he also contributed to the creation of the museum's video art collection, donating and placing twenty video artworks produced during that decade into the institution.
full.p7: In 2003 he participated in the XI Eugenio Mendoza Prize at Sala Mendoza, Caracas.
full.p8: In 2004 he presented the work Variations of the Eye. Videodance – Muu Blanco at the National Cinematheque of Caracas. That same year his work was included in the exhibition Electric Earth. Short Films and Videos from the UK and Venezuela, presented at Sala Mendoza, an international program dedicated to experimental video and short film.
full.p9: In 2006 he presented an experimental video project at the Jacobo Borges Museum, developed in collaboration with the Goethe-Institut. The project focused on street vendors and the informal economy in the streets of Caracas, addressing the urban landscape as a social and political space.
full.p10: Beginning in 2008 he started integrating expanded projection and video mapping into his multimedia installations. Later, in 2013, he developed a research project in slideshow and animated photographic portraiture, culminating that same year with his last solo exhibition in Venezuela, In Tha House, presented at Carmen Araujo Arte, a multimedia installation combining video, painting, sculpture, and sound.
full.p11: In 2014 he held his first solo exhibition in New York City with the multimedia installation Black Point Venezuela, presented within the performance program of Mandragoras Art Space in Long Island City. The work integrated sound art, video mapping, sculpture, and analog collage, addressing the social and political tensions of the contemporary Venezuelan context.
full.p12: That same year he moved to Miami, where he continues to develop much of his artistic production. In 2015 he presented Nuevo Pensamiento Compositivo Vol.1 at Arts Connection Foundation, within the Chill Concept space, an installation combining large-format photography, video mapping, and sound art.
full.p13: Between 2017 and 2019 he developed a series of experimental audiovisual events and experiences at Ironside Miami, specifically at Espacio Santamantis, where he organized gatherings dedicated to video mapping and live experimental music.
full.p14: Following the interruption of these creative spaces during the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2020 he co-founded the artistic collective IDArt Lab in the Allapattah neighborhood, active until 2023. Within this collective he participated in several group exhibitions presenting video mapping, experimental animations, and sound-responsive light performances accompanied by live sound art compositions.
full.p15: His most recent project is the installation and sound art program NatuUrban Symphony, presented between November 2024 and January 2025 at the Arts Connection Foundation, integrating experimental music, dance, video mapping projections, and the presentation of his documentary NatuUrban Symphony.
full.p16: Since 2017, Blanco has maintained the Instagram account @muublancovideoart as a living archive of his audiovisual production, documenting installations, performances, and video experiments developed during his last decade of work in Miami.
full.p17: With more than four decades of artistic trajectory, Muu Blanco has developed a hybrid practice in which video, sound, technology, and performance function as devices to investigate urban culture, memory, and contemporary social tensions. His work is part of various international public and private collections.

dossierbio.p1: Art, listening, the city, radio, television, DJ culture, music production, and multimedia practice: more than four decades of work, from La Cuadra, El Paraíso (Caracas, 1966) to Miami. The trajectory includes PARLAMENTO at the Sofía Imber Museum of Contemporary Art of Caracas, SHORT MUU and PARLAMENTO SONORO on 92.9 FM and La Mega 107.3 FM, DR. MUUSICA on Radio del Ateneo, residencies as a selector at BAR1 and 90 Grados, creative direction in television, and an ongoing practice as a multimedia conceptual artist, sound artist, music producer, and selector.
dossierbio.quote: “See, listen, record, select, archive, edit, and share.”

full.p2: The story of José Antonio Blanco Ángulo —Muu Blanco, DJ Muu, Dr. Muusica— begins in Caracas in 1966, in a family environment where the visual arts, architecture, literature, poetry, music, film, and technology were part of everyday life.
full.p3: The territory of origin had an affectionate name: La Cuadra, as they called Calle Este, next to what was then the Estadio Nacional El Paraíso, later known as Estadio Brígido Iriarte, in El Paraíso, Distrito Capital, Caracas, Venezuela.
full.p4: La Cuadra was the first territory of observation, companionship, friendship, street life, music, drawing, and memory from which Muu began to build his relationship with Caracas.
full.p5: A family genealogy crossed by art
full.p6: On his mother's side, Muu is the great-grandson of the Zulia poet Udón Pérez (Abdón Antero Pérez Machado), author of the lyrics of the Zulia State Anthem, chosen by competition and made official in 1909. This literary and poetic presence is part of a cultural genealogy that precedes his own artistic practice by several generations.
full.p7: Also on his mother's side, Muu was the grandson of Antonio Ángulo Luzardo, a figure linked early on to Venezuelan abstraction. On his father's side, his grandfather Antonio Blanco Peñalver was associated with domestic technology: he was the founder of Blanpeco, an appliance store and General Electric representative during the 1950s, with locations in downtown Caracas and Avenida San Martín.
full.p8: His father, Tony Blanco, was an architect and landscape designer. His mother, Milagros Ángulo de Blanco, built her professional life between Law and Psychology. Both loved the visual arts, poetry, ballet, music, and film.
full.p9: In that environment, Muu began to draw, paint, look at images, and listen to records. Paper, painting, architecture, books, photographs, films, and music formed a single field of experience from early on.
full.p10: The seventies: the house as a record library and visual workshop
full.p11: At his parents' house, listening to music was a daily ritual. The family collection brought together classical music, opera, film soundtracks, the Jackson 5, Julio Iglesias, bossa nova, flamenco, and a wide diversity of Venezuelan music, including Serenata Guayanesa, children's repertoire, and later Grupo Madera.
full.p12: Uncle Pradelio and young people's music
full.p13: During Christmases at his grandfather's house, another musical collection appeared. His maternal uncle Pradelio owned records associated with a younger generation, among them “Eva María se fue,” by La V Dimensión.
full.p14: Those visits showed him that each person owned a different collection, and that each musical archive could tell another story.
full.p15: Llovisna: salsa, calypso, and street music culture
full.p16: On the corner of La Cuadra lived one of his best childhood friends, known as Llovisna. His family came from Chapellín, in La Florida, and lived in an enormous multi-family house organized around a central patio with a huge mango tree.
full.p17: Salsa, calypso, and other tropical rhythms played there. Music had a direct social function: you had to dance. Muu learned salsa because dancing was part of community life and of his relationship with the neighborhood girls.
full.p18: Before British rock, post-punk, and electronic music came the salsa of the corner, an influence that would remain in his later work as a selector and producer.
full.p19: José Bousquet, “Diablo Rojo”: the recording laboratory
full.p20: His uncle by marriage José Bousquet, known as Diablo Rojo, owned an extraordinary home sound system and a reel-to-reel recorder.
full.p21: Muu began making long recordings with old records from his house and vinyl from his uncle's collection. The selections included Venezuelan pop, dance, soft rock, older repertoire, and international music. He would later reorganize those recordings onto cassette.
full.p22: Without knowing it, he was practicing operations that would become central to his work: recording, selecting, editing, and sequencing.
full.p24: Cassettes began to circulate outside the house. The boombox turned any space into a place of listening, especially during nighttime rides in the vans of his friend Enrique Montezuma.
full.p25: Muu's compilations accompanied those journeys and encounters. Before the museum, the club, and the radio, there already existed a practice of musical circulation based on discovering, selecting, recording, transporting, and sharing.
full.p26: Early 1980s: Raulito and the dark room
full.p27: Before Vista Alegre there was a fundamental musical friendship: Raulito —Raúl Blanco—.
full.p28: Muu and Raúl would lock themselves in his room, turn off the lights, turn up the volume, and listen. There Muu heard Pink Floyd for the first time, at high volume and in complete darkness. He also discovered U2's Red Rocks concert, The Police's “Roxanne,” DEVO's version of “(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction,” and other pieces that expanded his musical horizon.
full.p29: Raulito's room was his first experience of immersive, deep listening.
full.p31: Raúl Blanco introduced Muu to his friends from Calle 3 in Vista Alegre, among them the Chacín brothers, Caplis, and Chui. Raúl was also the older cousin of Horacio Blanco, who would later join that circle.
full.p32: Desorden Público would later emerge from that core group. Before the band, there was a community of friends devoted to exchanging music, images, and cultural references.
full.p34: Starting in 1984, gatherings became frequent. Vinyl, Betamax, VHS, music videos, concerts, album covers, clothing, new bands, and international scenes were all part of a collective practice of knowledge.
full.p35: During those years, Muu continued painting and drawing, while expanding his relationship with the visual arts. Music and image developed within the same sensibility.
full.p36: 1986: the beginning of a public trajectory in art
full.p37: Starting in 1986, Muu began actively participating in the Caracas art circuit through exhibitions, salons, actions, and experiences linked to the new contemporary scene.
full.p38: That same year he produced CALVO, during one of Desorden Público's first important concerts, at Estudio Mata de Coco. When it came time to perform the song, Muu walked on with a chair and sat down in the middle of the stage. After a musical introduction, Caplis approached and watched him; Danel Sarmiento began to sing, and Horacio Blanco proceeded to cut his hair.
full.p39: The song became the temporal structure of a bodily action. Music was beginning to function explicitly as artistic material.
full.p41: In 1987, Muu began attending Vertoche's parties — a music lover, underground DJ, and creator of the independent label 2 Extremo.
full.p42: Vertoche showed him the construction of a scene where music, fashion, design, identity, partying, and attitude converged. Their musical friendship lasted until the late 1990s.
full.p43: Years later, Vertoche would manage El 5 Combo, connecting with musicians close to Muu such as Pablo Estacio and Carlos Izzak, and with the circle of La Muy Bestia Pop, Chofa Loero, and Eduard Marshall.
full.p44: Late 1980s: Jhonny Ferreira / The Shaman One
full.p45: Another decisive influence was Jhonny Ferreira —The Shaman One—. Thanks to him, Muu discovered electronic music genres whose existence he had barely known. He began following him through various venues in Caracas, listening, observing, asking questions, and searching for records.
full.p46: Ferreira was first a reference, then a friend, and finally a colleague.
full.p48: In the late 1980s, Muu had his first extended experience playing music publicly, at L'Antro, in the Los Chaguaramos shopping center.
full.p49: It was the venue's last Friday in operation. Jhonny Ferreira would no longer be playing that week, but at DiscPlay much of the music he had bought and selected still remained. Muu took the booth for about five hours, reading through that collection, relating records to one another, building a sequence, and sustaining the energy of the night.
full.p50: L'Antro marked the transition between the music lover and the DJ.
full.p51: Early 1990s: Caracas as an analog network
full.p52: During the early 1990s, as the CD expanded, Muu constantly traveled around Caracas by metro and bus, carrying music, phone cards, and contacts.
full.p53: A phone call could end up at a friend's house: music would be played, food cooked, records exchanged, and conversations would go on for hours. The city functioned as an analog network of cultural circulation.
full.p54: At the same time, Muu continued taking part in the Caracas contemporary art circuit, among galleries, salons, museums, artists, curators, musicians, and designers.
full.p55: La Muy Bestia Pop: noise as material
full.p56: During that period, Muu maintained a close relationship with La Muy Bestia Pop. In one of their actions linked to the Nuevas Bandas circuit, he took part by generating sound with a grinder.
full.p57: An industrial tool became an instrument, and friction entered the music. This experience anticipated his later interest in sound art, soundscape, and field recording.
full.p59: Before having a program on 92.9 FM, Muu already had a relationship with the station through the visual arts. Together with Bubu Álvarez, he painted a large-format mural that covered walls and floors of the station's parking lot.
full.p60: The station would later be an important link for PARLAMENTO and SHORT MUU.
full.p62: In 1995, while accompanying his friends from Desorden Público to Sony Music's offices in Caracas, where they would meet about the artwork for the band's second album, En Descomposición, Muu found a promotional CD practically lying on the floor.
full.p63: The white cover, with black lettering, read: OPEN UP feat. JOHNNY ROTTEN — LEFTFIELD. On the cover there also appeared, in smaller type: AFRO-LEFT.
full.p64: When they listened to the CD on their Discmans, someone commented: “That's a banger.” Muu replied: “Give it to me. I'm keeping it.”
full.p65: The song would become a connecting point between his artistic activity, club culture, and radio.
full.p66: 1995: PARLAMENTO — second submission to the Salón Pirelli
full.p67: That same year, Muu submitted a proposal to the Salón Pirelli de Jóvenes Artistas for the second time. His first application had not been accepted. The new proposal was titled PARLAMENTO and was selected for the II Salón Pirelli de Jóvenes Artistas at the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Caracas Sofía Imber.
full.p68: The installation was centered on listening, conversation, technology, and human presence. It turned into a work a practice Muu had developed since childhood: bringing people together around music.
full.p70: PARLAMENTO was installed in the Sala Duchamp, whose thick wooden door had a central pane of glass and a lock. Muu kept the key and opened and closed the installation himself.
full.p71: Before opening hours, visitors could observe the space through the glass. On it was a sticker with the operating hours and the PARLAMENTO logo, created by Joaquín Urbina.
full.p72: The installation functioned like a small autonomous institution, with a name, a logo, hours, a key, programming, equipment, an archive, and guests.
full.p74: The project had the advisory support of curator Jesús Fuenmayor. Its graphic identity was developed together with Joaquín Urbina, from La Nacional, in Los Palos Grandes, a circle that also included Mirian Troconis, Iván Castillo, and Ernesto Rangel.
full.p75: New York People inside the museum
full.p76: For roughly the first month, PARLAMENTO featured a professional DJ display belonging to the miniteca New York People, courtesy of 92.9 FM. It included two Technics SL-1200 MKII turntables, a Rane mixer, and a Pioneer cassette recorder.
full.p77: A booth linked to Caracas nightlife thus physically entered the museum.
full.p79: The installation ran Tuesday through Sunday, roughly from 1:00 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. On the wall was a schedule of guests, among them Alejandro Rebolledo, Andrés Duque, Reinaldo Morales, Ivoly Noguera, Manuel Lebón, and José Antonio Hernández-Díez.
full.p80: They were not necessarily DJs, but rather artists and music lovers who brought music, talked with Muu, and listened together with the public.
full.p81: The encounters were recorded on cassette, and part of the situations were documented with a Video8 camera. The installation produced experience, a sound and audiovisual archive, and memory.
full.p82: From the museum to the club
full.p83: After the exhibition, Iván Gabaldón introduced Muu to Krikor Gazarian, who was looking for a different proposal from the conventional DJ for a new venue: a music-lover selector.
full.p84: Muu arrived with about ten CDs and did a thirty-minute test with Acid Jazz, Breakbeat, New Wave, Reggae, Drum & Bass, and, at one point, Afro-Left.
full.p85: Two weeks later he began working as a resident at BAR1, in La Castellana.
full.p87: At BAR1, Afro-Left became an emblematic piece. The bartenders would start their fire shows when it played and would ask him to repeat “la changa africana.” Muu could play it three or four times in a single night.
full.p88: Then came 90 Grados, at the CCCT, a period he remembers as his real musical university. He worked Wednesday through Saturday, from 8:00 p.m. to 3:00 a.m.
full.p89: The CD players had no pitch control, so he had to find other ways to relate songs to one another. Over thousands of hours in the booth, he developed a practice based on mixing apparently incompatible music.
full.p91: One night at 90 Grados, while Afro-Left was playing, a man kept insisting from outside the booth. Muu showed little interest until the visitor produced a card: Guillermo Zambrano, Executive Director, 92.9 FM.
full.p92: Zambrano asked who the artist of the song was. Muu showed him the Sony Music promotional CD. Zambrano offered him a radio program: “Kid, if you pass me that song, I'll give you a radio program. I always come here and you play amazing music that nobody else plays in Caracas.”
full.p93: Muu kept the card and called three days later.
full.p95: SHORT MUU — pasteurized and homogenized music was a roughly seven-minute radio micro-segment, broadcast on a rotating basis on Saturdays and Sundays on 92.9 FM.
full.p96: It marked the professional start of Muu's career in Venezuelan radio. The opportunity arose directly from his practice as a selector and from the circulation of a promotional CD that others had considered irrelevant.
full.p98: In 1997, Muu developed PARLAMENTO SONORO — DJ Muu on La Mega 107.3 FM, Fridays from 8:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., until the year 2000.
full.p99: The program carried the logic of the installation onto radio: a platform for listening, conversation, and musical circulation.
full.p100: Afterward, from 10:00 p.m. to midnight, Jhonny Ferreira / The Shaman One's show aired. The lineup closed the arc begun in the clubs: Muu, once a follower of Ferreira, now shared the same national radio night with him.
full.p102: In 1998, DJ Muu appears as associate producer of Código Demente, by La Corte. His activity was expanding into Venezuelan hip-hop and direct production.
full.p103: Later research into the history of Venezuelan hip-hop recognizes him as a DJ, communicator, and observer of the scene, with references to La Corte, Vagos y Maleantes, salsa, urban lyricism, and fusions.
full.p105: During those years, Muu took part in clubs, parties, warehouses, and events linked to Venezuelan electronic music. One later memory recalls him spinning at one of the raves held in a warehouse in Guarenas.
full.p106: Later, composer Miguel Noya would explicitly include DJ Muu in his academic chronology of Venezuelan electronic music.
full.p108: With several members of that scene, Muu took part in a DJ collective that circulated through Caracas venues and events. From that environment came the production of an electronic music CD for the HIT brand, distributed inside the DJEY fanzine, inserted in the El Nacional newspaper.
full.p110: Muu took part in SONOCLIPS, a music program on RCTV. The experience connected with the Betamax and VHS sessions of his adolescence, but now from inside a medium capable of bringing music videos and new music to a national audience.
full.p112: He later took part in ½ Hora Nacional, a space dedicated to showcasing Venezuelan audiovisual and musical production.
full.p113: From there he presented videos, bands, electronic music, fusions, and mestizo music. The program functioned as an instrument of cultural circulation and as a platform for making a scene visible.
full.p114: 2003: Música y Arte, un Solo Concepto
full.p115: In 2003, from 100.7 FM Radio del Ateneo de Caracas, Muu developed Música y Arte, un Solo Concepto (Music and Art, One Single Concept).
full.p116: The program synthesized a practice in which radio could function as exhibition, selection as curatorship, conversation as action, and recording as archive.
full.p118: Starting in 2003, Muu consolidated DR. MUUSICA on 100.7 FM Radio del Ateneo de Caracas. The name brought together the music lover, selector, collector, DJ, producer, artist, communicator, and researcher. It was not a character separate from Muu Blanco, but rather another way of presenting the same practice.
full.p119: Puma TV, Canal i, and creative direction
full.p120: After his initial stage in radio and music television, the story of ½ Hora Nacional connected with Puma TV's transition into what would later become Canal i.
full.p121: The institutional transition took place between 2004 and 2005. During that period, Muu Blanco took on greater responsibilities within the channel's structure for a few months and came to serve as creative director. The role brought together experience accumulated in image, music, video, design, programming, visual identity, and cultural production.
full.p123: In 2005, as Puma TV's transformation into the new television project that would later be identified as Canal i was consolidating, Muu sensed that the editorial, musical, and cultural direction was drifting away from the spirit he had defended.
full.p124: Faced with that institutional and creative transformation, he decided to resign. The departure marked the end of his television stage within that structure and reaffirmed his need to preserve conceptual autonomy when the medium no longer aligned with his research and his cultural ethics.
full.p126: Between 2007 and 2008, Muu's involvement in national electronic music production continued through projects such as Venezuela Electrónica.
full.p127: On Venezuela Electrónica Vol. 3 appears “Alba,” by Manuel Rangel and Muu Blanco, within the Mestizo line. The name describes a listening formed by classical music, salsa, rock, calypso, Venezuelan music, electronic music, hip-hop, and noise.
full.p128: 2009: Por el Medio de la Calle
full.p129: In 2009, DJ Muu took part in Por el Medio de la Calle, a Caracas gathering where the visual arts, music, performance, design, and urban intervention converged.
full.p131: Throughout this whole trajectory, Muu continued developing his practice within the visual arts through exhibitions, salons, actions, photography, video, installation, and performance.
full.p132: The experience accumulated in clubs, radio, television, and music production progressively led toward an investigation of sound as artistic material: field recording, soundscape, sampling, archive, electronic composition, multimedia installation, objects, video, performance, and ambient sound.
full.p133: His earliest reel-to-reel and cassette recordings already contained, intuitively, operations that would later reappear in sound art: recording, selecting, editing, sequencing, and sharing.
full.p135: Decades later, projects such as NatuUrban: A SubTropical Symphony of Miami bring together soundscapes, field recording, composition, living plants, and exhibition space.
full.p136: If PARLAMENTO introduced collective listening into the museum, NatuUrban expands that investigation toward incorporating a complete sonic territory within the exhibition space.
full.p138: The Selector persona remains active through historic vinyl records and repertoires that include Afro Latin Culture Flavor, Latin jazz, post-punk, New Wave, dub, funk, afrobeat, Mutant Disco, trip-hop, NY Freestyle, reggae, ska, and Acid Jazz.
full.p139: Each session functions as a temporary montage built out of records.
full.p141: For Muu, vinyl contains sound, design, technology, historical context, production, memory, and cultural information.
full.p142: The collection functions as an archive, and the set as a public activation of that archive.
full.p144: Thirty years after the encounter at Sony Music, Afro-Left returned to Muu's hands on vinyl.
full.p145: The song stopped being just a track and became a biographical document: an almost-discarded promotional CD had connected Sony Music, Desorden Público, PARLAMENTO, BAR1, 90 Grados, and 92.9 FM.
full.p146: More than four decades of professional practice
full.p147: Muu Blanco's trajectory spans more than four decades of activity across media and multimedia arts: multimedia conceptual artist, sound artist, music producer, selector, vinyl collector, DJ, radio and television communicator, creative director, performer, video artist, photographer, installation creator, soundscape researcher, beatmaker, and archivist.
full.p148: These activities are part of a single investigation into listening, image, memory, technology, and space.
full.p150: The trajectory can be read through a succession of media: family vinyl → reel-to-reel → cassette → boombox → Betamax/VHS → promotional CD → club booth → Technics SL-1200 MKII → Video8 → installation → FM radio → television → audiovisual creative direction → electronic production → digital archive → field recording → soundscape → multimedia installation.
full.p151: Each format expanded the scale of circulation and transformed the possibilities of the practice.
full.p153: 1966 — Born in La Cuadra, El Paraíso, Caracas.
full.p154: The seventies — Family music, drawing, painting, Uncle Pradelio's records, and first experiences of street listening with Llovisna.
full.p155: Late seventies and early eighties — José Bousquet “Diablo Rojo”: reel-to-reel, compilations, and first cassettes.
full.p156: Early eighties — Boombox, Enrique Montezuma's vans, and immersive listening with Raulito.
full.p157: After Raulito — Vista Alegre and the circle from which Desorden Público would emerge.
full.p159: 1986 — Beginning of sustained participation in exhibitions, salons, and artistic actions. Production of CALVO.
full.p161: Late eighties — Jhonny Ferreira and first long public session at L'Antro.

full.p177: Muu Blanco's trajectory begins with the drawings, the records at home, Uncle Pradelio, Llovisna, Diablo Rojo, the cassettes, Enrique Montezuma, Raulito, Vista Alegre, and the first communities of listening.
full.p178: It continues with Desorden Público, CALVO, Vertoche, Jhonny Ferreira, L'Antro, La Muy Bestia Pop, PARLAMENTO, BAR1, 90 Grados, radio, television, creative direction, electronic production, and soundscape.
full.p179: The child who drew and listened to records became an artist. The teenager who recorded reels and cassettes became a selector. The music lover reached the booth, the DJ entered the museum, and the installation expanded into radio, television, and multimedia production.
full.p180: More than four decades later, Muu Blanco continues developing a practice as a multimedia conceptual artist, sound artist, music producer, and selector. His work cannot be understood as the sum of separate careers, but rather as a continuous investigation into how to see, listen, record, select, archive, edit, and share.
full.p181: Technology changes, formats disappear, clubs close, radio stations and television channels transform, and archives age. Yet one question remains: what deserves to be seen, heard, remembered, and put back into circulation?

conceptual.lead: Four decades of artistic research where landscape, abstraction, sound, memory, nature, and technology converge to expand our perception of the contemporary world.

statement.p1: My artistic practice began in 1986 as an intuitive search that understood art not as an isolated discipline, but as a territory where image, sound, architecture, landscape, and memory could meet. Since then I have built a multidisciplinary trajectory in constant transformation, driven by the need to investigate how we perceive the world and how time reshapes our relationship with it.
statement.p2: I was born in Caracas in 1966, a city whose urban complexity deeply shaped my understanding of space. In my early years I developed a practice centered on painting, drawing, and experimental interventions, which soon evolved toward video art, experimental film, installation, and sound practices. In the nineties I received recognitions that reaffirmed this direction, among them the First Prize at the São Paulo Short Film Biennial for Perra Chillona and a Special Mention at the V National Art Biennial of Guayana.
statement.p3: My work has never answered to a single medium. Each project determines the language it needs in order to exist. Over four decades I have moved between photography, collage, musical composition, sound art, performance, documentary research, and immersive installations, understanding all of these disciplines as part of the same creative process.
statement.p4: Nature and landscape have been the permanent axis of my research. I do not conceive of them as scenery to be represented, but as living archives where history, ecology, culture, and human experience converge. From that exploration come projects such as Abstraciones Paisajísticas, Modernismo Anacrónico, NatuUrban: A SubTropical Symphony of Miami, and Archipiélago Sonoro, works that investigate the relationship between territory, memory, biodiversity, and sound.
statement.p5: Migrating to Miami in 2014 opened a new chapter in my practice. Encountering the subtropical ecosystems of South Florida broadened my interest in acoustic ecology and in the possibilities of creating immersive experiences where field recordings, electroacoustic composition, artificial intelligence, photography, video, and interactive technologies coexist. In this period, sound stopped accompanying the image and became a sculptural material capable of building spaces for contemplation.
statement.p6: During these years I have also developed intense work as a researcher, composer, Selector, editor, and cultural producer, generating publications, archives, vinyl records, concerts, labs, and outreach platforms dedicated to sound art and the musical cultures of the Caribbean and Latin America. I understand these activities as natural extensions of my artistic practice and as ways of activating communities around listening.
statement.p7: My work proposes a slowing down of looking and listening. I am interested in revealing what normally remains invisible: the resonances of landscape, the memories held within a territory, the everyday sounds that go unnoticed, and the hidden relationships between nature, city, and culture. Rather than represent a place, I seek to generate conditions to experience it from an expanded perception.
statement.p8: In 2026, marking forty years of artistic trajectory, I recognize that my work continues to be an open investigation. Each project is an invitation to listen differently, to observe more attentively, and to understand that landscape is not an external object, but a living organism of which we are also part. My practice continues to evolve between technological experimentation and poetic sensibility, convinced that art can build new forms of relationship with the world and with collective memory.

v1.p1: It is an active instance of a system where structure stops operating as containment and begins to behave as a surface of rupture.
v1.p2: In this context, sound does not function as composition, but as pressure: a force that crosses the limit until it tears it apart.
v1.track1title: Track 1 — (The Limit Tears / No One Stops)
v1.track1desc: It marks the moment the structure gives way. There is no transition or warning: the opening is immediate and total. What emerges does not follow a narrative logic, but a flow that recognizes neither brake nor direction.
v1.track2title: Track 2 — (They Breathe Where There Is No Air)
v1.track2desc: It inhabits the consequences of that rupture. Here, the anomaly stabilizes. The impossible does not collapse: it persists. What should have no conditions to exist finds a way to remain active within an environment that no longer distinguishes between inside and outside.
v1.p3: The work does not propose a story, but a state: a zone where perception is forced to operate without stable references.
v1.closing: ARGMUU does not construct meaning; it subjects it to interference.

v1.p1: It represents a synthesis of images made by Muu Blanco (Caracas, Venezuela, 1966) centered on the confluence of nature, architecture and other forms that embrace the sensitive tradition of geometric abstraction present in Venezuelan art.
v1.p2: The genesis of the project is inscribed in the emergence of the experimental learning space conceived by the Instituto de Estudios Superiores de Artes Plásticas Armando Reverón (IUESAPAR): practice and critique of contemporary systems of visual representation. There, significant dialogues took place with researcher Sandra Pinardi, curator Luis Enrique Pérez Oramas and architect William Niño Araque, which shaped the creative circumstances to advance this visual research.
v1.p3: The images that make up this particular series refer to the so-called Escuela de Caracas, the movement that inaugurates Venezuelan visual modernity. The unifying presence of the Ávila's forms represents a visual center of gravity that imposes counterpoints on the ways of looking at the city as an experience of looking at ourselves.
v1.p4: Likewise, the encounter with architecture is a strongly present trait and captures the conception of a new monumentality, connected to a sensibility that revitalizes the integrative experience of art and architecture, now in clear reference to the agonic, vital, dynamic and complex dimension of the place. The emergence of light and the symbolic prominence of the sky — perhaps as a connection to colonial memory, Caracas as a branch of heaven? — also constitutes a significant reference within the montage of images that make up this series.

v3.p1: In this case, I have intervened, with pills of personal medication, Paolo Gasparini's photographic book Retromundo, edited in Venezuela in 1986.
v3.p2: I understand my work with this book as a conceptual action. I am interested in exploring reflexively the elements that integrate and configure my daily world and its flux with my life experiences. I do not do that from an intimate perspective. On the contrary, I do it from an archeology of self (the pills I take every day can convert themselves into archeological personal remains).
v3.p3: From this point, my artistic work searches for a transgressive and contingent dialogue with the particular discourses of Latin American modernities and, specifically, with those inscribed in the context of Venezuelan history. My photographic compositions with pills placed on fragments of the book Retromundo do not articulate or display an epic or nostalgic regard on the visions of the author of the original photographs. They are, rather, aesthetic fissures. The pills function as factors of association with the personal world of anyone. They are samples of an altered modernity.
v3.details: Fine art photography · 13×20 cm · 30 pages · ISBN 9781367872233 · Published April 2016 · English

v4.p1: Now, in the Venezuelan case, it is no longer about a Land of Grace, as Cristopher Columbus would put it in the chronicles of his trips to the New World. The modern utopias anchored in the ideals of a cornucopian nature have been transformed, with the sudden and intensive exploitation of the underground mineral resources, into real individual and collective tragedies. The recent history of Venezuela bears witness to this: a nation that, in spite of holding the biggest oil reserves in the world, has not been able to warrant economic growth and social equity to its citizens.
v4.p2: From this perspective, Muu Blanco proposes to invert the Venezuelan oil imaginary through the series New Compositional Thinking (2014). In this work, Blanco carries out an intervention on a set of images referring to the Venezuelan oil epic, first published in the photography magazine Extra Cámara, by inserting a scapular bearing the effigy of Chapulín Colorado. No doubt, the intention of such an insertion is that the spectator recalls the famous TV character's phrase: "And now, who will defend us?" At the same time, it is evident that with this work Muu Blanco denounces the cult of oil in the same way that the historian Germán Carrera Damas exposed some years back the cult of Bolívar, so deeply entrenched in Venezuelan culture.

natuurban.videoDesc: A documentary short directed by Jacopo Fantastichini and produced by PlantPop, curated by Gerardo Zavarce. It follows Muu Blanco's career and the creation process of his sound art installation NatuUrban Symphony, which explores the natural and urban sounds of national parks on the outskirts of major South Florida cities — an installation made possible through the sponsorship of Arts Connection Foundation, with whom Muu Blanco has collaborated in Miami since 2014. The film features imagery by Camera Creature SVC and original music by Dr.Muusica, documenting the work's central concept: live plants holding mini speakers that play soundscapes connecting the natural and the urban. It premiered on July 30, 2025 at SilverSpot Cinemas, Downtown Miami, as part of the FilmGate Festival — Muu Blanco's first documentary short made in the United States, a milestone within his forty years of uninterrupted artistic career.

tizon.medium: Video art · 03:33 min · MiniDV/NTSC · Director: José Antonio Blanco Angulo · Cinematography, editing and original music: Muu Blanco
tizon.p1: The Torres de Parque Central are one of Caracas's icons, a symbol of the city's opening to modernity in the 1970s. For Caraqueños, these towers give the city its character: a chaotic and passionate character, the immortal maiden of the Ávila. For Muu Blanco, the creator of this short film, witnessing the fire in the east tower of Parque Central sparked an immediate reflection on the meanings held by this urban protagonist.
tizon.intro: The title of this short film comes from the Spanish word «tizón». A tizón is: 1. A half-burnt stick. 2. A stain on one's reputation or self-esteem. From these two notions arises the title of this work, charged with symbolic meaning.
tizon.p2: At another time, it had been his «playground» (his father was part of the team of architects who built the complex, passing on to him an emotional bond with the work).
tizon.p3: The artist interprets this event as an image of the sociopolitical moment Venezuelans were living through at the time; as a reflection of the deterioration of their society. A stain on the self-esteem of its citizens. A refusal to be consumed by the tizón of their politics and their decline.
tizon.p4: This short film (03:33 minutes long) was produced on MiniDV format and edited on a Mac PowerBook G4, using original music by Muu Blanco aka Jaba Lee Project, who incorporates for this piece a fragment of the orchestra «La Billo's Caracas Boys» (a well-known Venezuelan ensemble of the 1950s). That track was remixed to produce a dynamic, repetitive rhythm that plays against the images of Caracas as a half-burnt «tizón».

v3.meta: Concept and curation: Muu Blanco · Doral Cultural Arts Center (DIAF 1), 2023 / Arts Connection Foundation, November 2023
v3.desc: This historical overview, spanning from Futurism to contemporary Sound Art, highlights the evolution of sound experimentation throughout the XX and XXI centuries. Beginning with Futurist artists who sought to represent modern life and technology through chaotic Dadaism and musical vanguards such as Concrete Music and Fluxus. Next, Radio Art introduces collaboration and audience interaction into the audible narrative. Lastly, Ambient Music, inspired by Brian Eno, focuses on creating relaxing sound atmospheres. Finally, R. Murray Schafer's Soundscape concept highlights the importance of sounds in culture and the environment, influencing urban design and environmental awareness. This historical journey reflects the constant expansion of sound creativity over the years.

v1.meta: Live multimedia action · Opening of the group exhibition of New World School of the Arts students and graduates, Miami Dade Art District — Miami Art Week 2025
v1.p1: It is a live multimedia action that explores the intersection of landscape, body and technology through a continuous flow of sound and image. Over 30 minutes, the intervention articulates a dialogue between synthesizer, beat, live radio, trombone and a visual device that blends loops of moving water —filmed off the coast of Key Biscayne— with digital drawings transformed into kaleidoscopic patterns through MadMapper.
v1.p2: This visual cartography is joined by dynamic, vibrating lines, generated in real time, that react to the sound frequencies created during the action. These lines respond not only to the synthesizer, the beat or the trombone: the noise of the audience also becomes a visual trigger, integrating into the system so that every vibration, every murmur and every ambient interruption modifies the projection. The audience thus becomes an involuntary co-author of the piece, leaving a trace inscribed in the texture of the image.
v1.p3: The work builds a sensory ecosystem where the natural and the digital influence each other: acoustic vibration runs through the visuality, the marine landscape is fragmented and expanded, and the collective presence becomes part of the pulse that sustains the experience. The radio transmission introduces an element of chance and live presence, underscoring that every shore —physical or technological— is a point of crossing.
v1.p4: Presented at the opening of the group exhibition of New World School of the Arts students and graduates in the Miami Dade Art District, as part of Miami Art Week 2025, the action proposes an immersive territory where sound, image and audience coexist in a state of continuous vibration.

v2.meta: Sound action · PINTA Art Fair, Miami Art Week 2025
v2.p1: I appear faceless, covered by a nest of magnetic tape: remnants of voices, fractured memories, recordings no one listens to anymore. My instrument is a green trombone, the color of sprout and toxicity, of hope and rust. With it I blow a language that seeks not music, but fissure.
v2.p2: This sound action is a gesture of insubordination. Atonal, repetitive, insistent: a refusal of the structures that domesticate the ear and the discourses that order the body. What happens here is not a concert, but an interruption. Not a spectacle, but an open crack in the flow of what is supposed to be seen, celebrated, consumed.
v2.p3: In this marina garden, guarded by boats awaiting their departure to sea, I become interference. I bring with me the vibrations of a scattered south, of migrant geographies, of cities that rethink themselves from their margins. I blow from the silences that have not been invited, from the memories that resist being archived, from the fragility of what persists even when everything tries to erase it.
v2.p4: The infinite repetitions do not seek hypnosis, but affirmation: to exist is to insist. In front of the fair, in front of the market, in front of the logic that labels, values and circulates, I present a presence that refuses to be captured. My sound does not offer melody, it offers detour. It does not offer relief, it offers possibility.
v2.p5: I invite you to listen without expecting. To remain without understanding. To accompany this act as one who enters a wave that does not belong to them, but still touches them. May this vibration remind us that the indeterminate also has the right to occupy space.

v3.meta: M/P'25 · Edge Zone Cultural Center, Miami
v3.p1: "Ceguera Ambiental y SocioCultural Vol.1 (Miami)" belongs to the line of artistic research Muu Blanco has developed for more than two decades, where the sonic, the political and the visual intertwine in actions that interrogate the tensions of contemporaneity.
v3.p2: This project engages in dialogue with the artist's previous experiences, such as his urban sound actions in Caracas, where the noise of the city was transformed into plastic and performative material; his critical audiovisual installations on violence and power, in which media language became a field of distortion and resistance; as well as his explorations under the alias DrMuusica, in which vinyl, loop and improvisation rewrite the sound archives of the Caribbean and its diaspora.
v3.p3: In all these approaches, Blanco has sought the same gesture: to reconfigure the signs of the everyday, the political and the cultural into sensory landscapes where memory, tension and the urgency of our time are activated. Ceguera Ambiental y SocioCultural continues this critical and experimental path, now with a radical emphasis on perception itself: geometric lines and sound vibrations that, when intertwined, reveal the contemporary contradiction between the rigidity of the social gaze and the uncontrollable power of improvisation and error.

calvo.title: CALVO
calvo.medium: Performance · Estudio Mata de Coco, Caracas, Venezuela · December 6, 1986
calvo.p1: CALVO, Muu Blanco's first public performance, held on December 6, 1986 at Estudio Mata de Coco, Caracas, during Desorden Público's first major concert.
calvo.p2:
1986: the body enters the work.
2026: memory allows us to recognize the reach of that gesture.

essay.p1: CALVO takes place on December 6, 1986 at Estudio Mata de Coco, Caracas, during Desorden Público's first major concert. When the moment comes to begin the song "Calvo," Muu Blanco walks onto the stage with a chair, places it at the center, and sits facing the audience. A musical introduction begins. Caplis approaches, watching him with bewilderment, as if trying to understand what is happening. Then Danel Sarmiento begins singing "Calvo" and Horacio Blanco approaches Muu to cut his hair in front of the audience. Once completely bald, Muu Blanco rises, performs a ska-punk dance on stage, and finally leaps into the audience.
essay.p2: Over time, the artist would recognize this event as his first public action and his first performance: a foundational experience that changed his relationship to art and to the body as a territory of creation.
essay.p3: Seen from the present, CALVO appears as an action built from a precise sequence: appearance, waiting, transformation, movement, and rupture of the stage space. Its power does not come from a complex staging or a previously explained narrative, but from the way a concrete gesture unfolds before the audience and acquires meaning within the concert.
essay.p4: The chair introduces a pause in the midst of the musical energy. Muu Blanco sits down and remains exposed, motionless, while the situation begins to acquire an unexpected tension. Caplis's gaze underscores that bewilderment and makes visible the irruption of something not yet fully defined as concert, theater, or performance.
essay.p5: When the song begins, the title "Calvo" ceases to function only as a word and becomes a material action. As Danel sings, Horacio Blanco physically transforms Muu's appearance in front of everyone. The body does not represent the word: it embodies it.
essay.p6: Music thus fulfills a structural function. It marks the time of the action, accompanies the transformation, and activates the passage from stillness to movement. Once the cutting is finished, Muu leaves the chair and enters the rhythm. The ska-punk dance breaks the initial containment and leads to the leap into the audience, with which the traditional separation between stage and audience momentarily disappears.
essay.p7: That displacement — from the chair to the stage and from the stage to the audience — is central to understanding the piece. CALVO begins with a body isolated at the center of the scene and ends with that same body immersed in the collective.
essay.p8: The initial idea for the action came from Roberto Fuentes Anzola, then artistic producer of Desorden Público and remembered by Muu Blanco as a friend and beloved mentor. This collaborative origin is essential to understanding the genealogy of the work. CALVO is born within a network of creative and musical complicities, but acquires its performative dimension in the way Muu Blanco takes on the proposal and carries it through to its bodily and scenic consequences.
essay.p9: Seen from 2026, forty years later, CALVO can be recognized as a point of origin within the artist's trajectory. Not because it programmatically announces all his subsequent production, but because it establishes early on a relationship between body, sound, time, action, and public presence that will reappear, through other media, throughout his work.
essay.p10: It also raises a question that will remain relevant throughout his practice: what happens when the artistic experience ceases to be contained in an object and comes to depend instead on a situation lived in real time?
essay.p11: In 1986, that question was not yet formulated as theory. The experience came first. First there were the chair, the music, the cut, the dance, and the leap. The reading came afterward.
essay.p12: That is why CALVO can be understood today as something more than an anecdote tied to one of Desorden Público's first important moments and to the Caracas music scene of the 1980s. It is the instant in which Muu Blanco publicly discovers that his own body could become matter, support, and artistic event.
essay.p13: In that sense, CALVO is a point zero.
essay.p14:
1986: the body enters the work.
2026: memory allows us to recognize the reach of that gesture.

soundart.title: Exploring the Roots and Evolution of Sound Art
soundart.desc: A solo exhibition tracing a genealogy of sound art, from Futurism to the 21st century, presented at Miami International Fine Art (MIFA) between 2023 and 2025. The project combines sound installation pieces, historical documentation, and original work by Muu Blanco, situating his practice within a broader tradition exploring sound, technology, and space. The show was also presented in a Doral variant, expanding its reach and consolidating one of the artist's most sustained curatorial investigations into the history of sound art.

ceguera.title: Ceguera Ambiental y SocioCultural Vol.1 (Miami)
ceguera.desc: A performance addressing environmental and sociocultural blindness as a contemporary condition, the first installment of a series developed in Miami during 2025. The piece combines body, sound, and critical gesture to question the relationship between perception, environment, and collective responsibility. It belongs to Muu Blanco's ongoing performance practice, active within Miami's performance art circuit, and is documented on video within the site's Projects archive.

modernismo.title: Modernismo Anacrónico
modernismo.desc: A series of collage, assemblage, and installation work begun in 2002 and active to this day. The project gathers photographs of pieces built from found materials and mixed techniques, published as an eponymous art book and also presented at the international SWAB fair (2008). Modernismo Anacrónico proposes an ironic dialogue between the modern promise and its material remains, one of the earliest and most sustained lines of Muu Blanco's visual practice, fully documented in the Projects gallery.

afrolatin.title: Afro Latin Culture Flavor
afrolatin.meta: Fanzine · Selector residency 2024–2026 · Tripping Animals Brewery, Doral
afrolatin.desc: A monthly printed fanzine, limited edition, edited and produced by Muu Blanco / Dr.Muusica, published in Doral City, Miami. From 2024 to 2026, the project ran alongside a weekly Selector residency as sound researcher at Tripping Animals Brewery, where Dr.Muusica presented vinyl sessions under the name Dr.Muusica Selector. Afro Latin Culture Flavor connects editorial practice with live music selection, exploring Afro-Latin roots, rhythm, and popular culture as a real-time sonic archive.

workwithmuu.lead: Available for exhibitions, performances, site-specific sound commissions, talks, and vinyl listening sessions. Forty years of interdisciplinary practice between Caracas and Miami.

soundart.title: Sound Art & Performance
soundart.desc: Live sound performance, expanded sound installations, and improvisation for galleries, festivals, and public spaces.

commissions.title: Site-Specific Sound Commissions
commissions.desc: Original sound pieces developed for a specific space, exhibition, or site — ambient composition, video mapping, spatial audio.

talks.title: Artist Talks
talks.desc: Talks and presentations on sound art, video art, and forty years of interdisciplinary practice, with an exhibition history spanning the Americas and Europe — from Caracas and Miami to New York, Madrid, Venice, and São Paulo.

vinyl.title: Vinyl Listening Experiences
vinyl.desc: Curated vinyl listening sessions and Selector sets exploring Afro-Latin, experimental, and archival sound — from intimate gatherings to public events.
